utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you took on the last occasion that you were here; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm afraid your answer was not heard. I don't think the microphones are -- can he be heard?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. This is a voice distortion case, isn't it? I'm afraid the technicians will have to sort this one out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can the interpreters switch to the right channel, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The right channel is 7.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the witness please say some numbers or words into the microphone, whatever you want to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, you are taking your witness in chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just one moment. I'm sorry, I've forgotten. We are in a different courtroom. Mr. Krnojelac, are you able to understand the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. Sit down, please, sir. Sorry, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when we -- when you started your testimony, you mentioned that fighting stopped after a few days in Foca. Do you recall when it stopped, what date it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the attack on Foca started on the 8th of April. That lasted for a few days, four or five days, and then it abated a bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did the Muslims do when the fighting stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started leaving Foca en masse. There were massive columns of people across the bridge on the Drina River and in the direction of Gorazde, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Muslim houses in Donje Polje during the fighting or after the fighting had stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the houses started burning, and throughout that time houses were burning, Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "started burning," how did they start to burn? Was it during the fighting activities or did they start to burn otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both during combat operations and later, when things abated. They were setting houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did. I saw houses on fire, but I could not say whose house was on fire, which house was on fire exactly, because I didn't dare look back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But how, then, do you know that they were Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about it from these people in prison later. I heard whose houses had turned down. We talked amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the 11 mosques in Foca that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today there's not a single one left. All of them were either burned down or mined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the fighting ceased, did the people resume work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they did not. Muslims did not work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't dare. They weren't allowed to get into the company where they worked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any general restrictions on movements? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were, out of fear, for the most part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there also any official restrictions, like announcements or orders that did allow movements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they imposed a curfew in the evening. It would start in the evening and you were not supposed to move about, at least that's what they said on the radio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These restrictions, were they equally directed against all ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at home, was it ever searched, your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there, no, while I was in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had hunting weapons. I was a member of the hunting association.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep this weapon throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Until the 15th of April it was at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And what happened on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, a police car went through town, providing information as follows: that everybody who had weapons was supposed to bring it out to the plateau in front of the Ribarski Dom, and that all Muslims and Serbs should go out to this plateau, to this square.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you go there with your weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened on this plateau?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this plateau there were a couple hundred of men, women, and children. Serbs and Muslims had to get out there. While we were waiting, we saw from the direction of the army building, we saw some soldiers in black uniforms walking down the street, armed with automatic weapons. They were walking towards this group that had gathered in front of this fish restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do with your weapon, and what happened to the other weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all had to put weapons down on the sidewalk; we had to line them up. And when they came, they said, "Whose weapons are these?" and then all of us who had permits said that it was us. And then they divided the Serbs from the Muslims; Serbs on the one side and all the others on the other side. They collected our weapons and returned their weapons to them, I mean those who had brought them out, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "their" and "them," you need to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told the Serbs to take their weapons and to take them home, but they took ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone arrested on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's when they started taking some of the Muslims out of that group. They took 15 men; they handcuffed them; they hit them; they put them into some kind of a vehicle, a kombi van; and they took them in a direction unknown to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of some of these 15 men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, Murat Crneta, Zulfo Veiz, Munib Veiz, Uzeir Aganovic, Adil Krajcin, et cetera. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has just mentioned Munib Veiz, that is Schedule C-28; he mentioned Zulfo Veiz, that is C-29; he mentioned Adil Krajcin, that is C-14; and Uzeir Aganovic is also on the list. I forgot to note down. It's also from Schedule C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He mentioned the other Veiz as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I have mentioned. Munib 28 and Zulfo 29.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, was there a particular reason to single these 15 men out? Could you see a reason why them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I could not. Nobody could understand that, according to which criterion they singled them out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see these men again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them in prison down there. And they told me that they were first taken to the prison Livade, called Solana [phoen], and they beat them there, mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "they," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs. They beat Munib Veiz there at the plateau when they first took him away and later when they brought him to Livade, and Zulfo Veiz as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you arrested, and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 23rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean at your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, some four men in uniform came. Among them I recognised only one. It was a Pipovic from the village of Celebic. He used to go to high school; he was a student of mine. They came banging at the door and asking whose apartment this was. My wife went out and said whose apartment this was. And they asked where I was, and she said that I was in the apartment. I got out and they asked me, "Have you got any weapons?" and I said that I had weapons with a permit and that I handed them over to the so-called Serb military police on the 15th of April. "Have you got more weapons?" they asked me, and I said, "Please search the apartment. If you find any weapons, you kill me." And this Pipovic said that he knew me and that he didn't want to go and search the apartment. And I asked, "Would you like to have a drink?" and they said that I should bring a drink out to them there in the staircase. I brought them drinks, they had a drink, and they left. I watched from the window, from behind the curtain. They got out of the building, all four of them. And in the meantime, from the direction of the army building, a few luxury cars appeared and on them it said "Military Police." They stopped there in front of Ribarsko. Dragan Cosovic, nicknamed Cosa, got out of the first car. Later on I found out is that he was the commander of this military police. And I saw that he called to these four guys who were at my place and said something to them, and then two of them returned later, pointed at my building, and two out of the four returned to my place again. They came to my door and said, "We're sorry, but you have to come with us to give a statement."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took me into a white Golf car in front of the entranceway, and they said that they were taking me to the SUP, to the police, to make a statement. However, when I asked whether I had to get ready, they said, "No, no, you will be coming back immediately. You're just supposed to make a statement and then you'll go straight back home." However, when I got into the car, they did not go to the police at all, they did not go in that direction. They went across the bridge. I kept silent in the car. Then they took me to the KP Dom, to in front of the KP Dom -- to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two and a half years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they ever tell you why you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know the way it was. Everybody who was brought to the KP Dom had to make a statement, some kind of a statement, had to be interrogated. When I was brought, I was put into a room -- am I supposed to tell you about that as well?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to know first. Have you ever been charged or convicted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's now move on into the KP Dom. When you arrived, who received you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in front of the entrance of the KP Dom, one of these guys who was in the car got out and said to the driver - I mean both of them were in camouflage uniforms - he said that I should stay in the car until he went to the administration to see something. He stayed there for about five minutes and then he came back and he ordered me to get out of the car. I got out of the car. There was a group of men there at the entrance in front of the front door. I noticed Cedo Skipin; he was president of the court in Foca. And said -- he addressed me by my name and he said, "How come you're here?" And I said, "Well, they brought me to make some kind of statement." He turned to the other side, and then I was taken through this detector. I had two packs of cigarettes in my pockets, and I passed through this other gate, the metal gate. A guard was there, the former guard of the KP Dom, Veljko Kovac, and he told me to go there to the compound. He opened the door for me and he said that I should report to Slavko Koroman. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you report to Mr. Koroman? And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. When I got into this compound where these buildings are for prisoners, I looked around. It's a big compound. And over there in front of the dining hall I saw Slavko Koroman because I knew him. And I started walking towards him. However, from both buildings people started coming to the windows because as soon as they'd bring someone in, people would gather around the windows to see who had been brought in. I got lost then. I saw this Koroman. I started walking towards him. He saw me going there and then he started approaching me too, and he said, "How come you're here?" and I said to him, "Well, yes, to make a statement." And he said, "This is no good. This is no good that they've brought you here."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why it would not be good to be brought there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, nothing. He said, "I have to put you up in a room." "What kind of room?" He stood and looked at me and he said, "The best would be for me to put you into Room 15. It's the sunniest of all." That's the only thing he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Room 15, where was it in the building? Do you recall which floor it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third floor. It was on the third floor, in the first building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "third floor," do you mean the top floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In that place, it's the highest one of them all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Room 15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed until the autumn, sometime around October, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the guard came once and told me to collect my things and to go to this other building, to number 18.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Room 18, on which floor was this room; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in number 18?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there -- I think I stayed there until the summer 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just clarify something. When you say "second floor," do you mean the floor above the ground floor or do you mean the ground floor, first floor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We've got a bigger problem than that because this building had something called the ground floor and then there was a floor underneath it. It really should not be difficult to sort this one out with a leading question, unless there's some real dispute about it. He's been using what I would call the American system so far, if you count the basement as the basement. But because the building -- how about a photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I'm having this photograph now and want to put it to the witness so that he can show us all the rooms he was in. With the help of -- oh, the usher is gone. It's the photograph 7512 of Exhibit 18.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Do you want me to leave it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the upper photo and show us first, where was the Room 15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 15 was over here, between the first and second building. Over here on the corner. Here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means it's not the top floor, it's actually the third floor counting the basement as the first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The third floor, and then up here was the prison clinic, the prison hospital, as it was called, up here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, to clarify it, would you please put the pointer on Room Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 15 so that we can see which floor you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's not a very good photograph for that, is it, because it's behind a tree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see 15. You can't. It's in the corner here between this other building and this first building. In the corner here, you can't see those windows. It would be here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I think it's clear that he pointed on the second floor above the ground floor. And we don't have -- actually, we don't have a better photo than this one. But I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understood him to be saying that Room 15 was on the floor below the medical rooms. Now, if I've misunderstood it, perhaps we better sort it out. But he was on -- not the top floor, but the one below the top floor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, below. Let me show you here. In the basement was Room 12, and then above it was 14, and above it was 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Would you now point out to us where Room 18 was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please use the same photo, 7512. I think it's easier to show it there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is pointing at the first floor above the basement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, he's not. It depends on what you call --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: To me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basement is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. You go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And into which room were you taken after being in Room 18?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After number 18, we were transferred here, to 16, and then 13. We were then returned to this building again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Room 16, that's directly below 18; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Room 13, you mentioned it's above 11; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can put the photo away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Room 15, were there already other detainees there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The room was full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a smaller room. Those are the smallest rooms, 14 and 15. There were about 40 men there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "men." Does that mean there were only male people in this room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a five-year-old girl.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did the five-year-old girl get there, into KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they captured her father at home. He could not leave her at home so he brought her with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there enough space for these 40 people in the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of those who happened to be there took the beds; others, on the floor. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity did the people have in Room -- in your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned already the little girl. What age were the people in the room? Who was the eldest, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, she was five years old, and then up to the age of 70 or 80, there were persons of that age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know these people from before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew most of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were civilians. Civilians only. Not a single one was a -- not a single one was a military man. I mean, nobody wore a uniform. All were brought from their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What state of health were these people in? Were there any sick people among you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were. There were people they brought from hospitals in pyjamas who were lying in hospital beds before that, and they brought them there straight from there. Juso Cebo was a man who had a lung condition and who had spent a long time in hospital, and that's the way they brought him to the KP Dom. There were also mentally disturbed people; there were disabled persons; there were elderly persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned already that you could see when you arrived that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there were other people in other rooms. Could you estimate how many detainees were there altogether in the first few months?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could only count when we were going to the canteen, and people would stand at the windows and count, although it was forbidden to stand at the window. But people did it somehow and did the counting and then made their calculations on a piece of paper. The number varied; it was never the same. Some people were brought in; other people were taken away. And when we did the calculations, there would be about 800 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know many of these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they civilians, or were soldiers among them or fighters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were civilians, except in 1993, they brought one man from Rogoj who had been captured there, and he was in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any women and children detained in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were, but they kept them there for only a short time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beside the prisoner rooms you have mentioned, were also detainees kept in other rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in solitary cells, the so-called solitaries, as they called them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you estimate how many detainees were kept in those isolation cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who had been in isolation cells and were later released back to their rooms would tell us that there had been 13 to 15 people in an isolation cell at a time. They couldn't sit down; there was standing room only. And there were people who had spent months in isolation cells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever taken into an isolation cell yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of detainees were kept in the isolation cells?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually when they brought people in just before dark, they would keep them in isolation cells before they -- before taking a statement from them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you looked out of the window of Room 15, at what did you look? What could you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could see the administration building where they took us to the so-called interrogations, and we could see those rooms where they took people and where we all had to go to those interrogations. From that room you can see the entrance of the compound to the administration building and the administration building itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to show you two photos; that is, photo 7477 first, and I would like you to tell us if that was about the view you had. If you look at the bottom photo, would that be the view you had from Room 15, about? About.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was precisely the view we had, and we could see this part as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you see the three --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, sorry. This is the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just look at the bottom photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look only at the bottom photo. These three windows that you see on the ground floor next to this metal door, left from the metal door, what kind of rooms were they; do you know? What kind of rooms were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, those were visitation rooms used for visits to inmates. And later this is where our people, the Muslims, were taken to be interrogated and maltreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to this later on. I would like you to look at another photo now, and it's the photo 7472. Please have a look at this photo, and can you tell us if -- from Room 15, could you see the Drina River, or were you below?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we could not see the Drina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Witness, are you familiar with the KP Dom? Did you ever visit it before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had been there several times in the administration building, not anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been in the room of the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the room of the warden was? Which floor, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the second floor. There is a ground floor, then another floor, and this was on the floor above, the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the floor plan 6/3. Can you put it the other way around. Could you turn it. No, it's okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is supposed to be the second floor. Can you show us the warden's room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the big room --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at the room that everybody else has identified as the warden's room. I don't think that this is really in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The only problem is that we sometimes have witnesses who say they met the warden in a different room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's quite different to "What was the warden's room?" Everybody, I think, has agreed that that is the warden's office, if that is the right word for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were there guards in the KP Dom while you were detained there? And if so, who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was brought there, only the former guards, security people, of the KP Dom worked there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they wear and how were they armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning there was a great diversity - some were in camouflage uniforms; some were in other uniforms; some were in civilian clothes - but later they all wore police uniforms. And as to how they were armed, they had automatic rifles, pistols; some of them carried knives, and all of them had clubs, batons; some of them even had bombs on them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever see a machine-gun in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a machine-gun on the -- at the window of the administration building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which part of the administration building, the right wing or the left wing when you look at it from your room, number 15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the left wing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the compound mined while you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire compound was mined, and we saw them laying the mines from the windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that done, and who did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in May, the mining. I recognised three of the mining squad; that was Miodrag Vracar, who earlier worked in the municipal assembly; Zelimir Troje, who had been a lecturer in a school, in a secondary school; and Bozo Sain, who was a mechanic in an auto repair shop. And there were a couple of other people whom I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they soldiers at that time? Were they wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were wearing uniforms, soldiers' uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were only Muslims detained in KP Dom or people of other ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were others too. We had Croats with us, and in other rooms there were Serbs as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Serbs were detained in the KP Dom, and where were they detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept them in building 2, and I don't know how many because I don't know the number. Sometimes there would be a lot of them and sometimes the number would be smaller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they kept separate from the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the room, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know in which room the Serbs were kept, which number this room had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While we were in Room 18, they were in Room 21. And there was only a staircase between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of persons were these Serb prisoners? Were they convicts or were they normal people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were civilians among them, but most of them were in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of living conditions did they have? Were you able to tell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for accommodation, I believe their situation was similar to ours, although they had more blankets and they had bed sheets; most of us didn't. They would have more bedding in the winter than we. The food was much better -- their food was much better. Our food was prepared outdoors, in a big cauldron, and we would get our rations in small dishes in which former inmates got their salads, and that was the amount of our rations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that the Serbs got more -- the Serb prisoners got more than you? Could you see it, or how do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could see that. They prepared food for them inside, in the kitchen, and even humanitarian aid would arrive sometimes. They would unload the foodstuffs into the storage room. Below Room 16 there was a big storage room there. Our people, Muslims, would be taken there to unload. And food was prepared for them from the foodstuffs from the humanitarian aid, and we would get cabbage. And everyone lost from 20 to 40 kilos in the first couple of months. I lost 31 kilos in that period. I couldn't stand on my feet; I fainted several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "we," you mean the detainees, the Muslims and the Croats, and not the Serbs; is that what we have to understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the conditions in winter? You already mentioned that the Serbs had more blankets. How were the conditions of the other detainees during the winter, especially the first winter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was terrible that first winter because there were no window panes. Most of them were broken. For a long time we were in those rooms. We were not able to get warm. They had taken away our blankets, all but one thin blanket, and the winter was horribly harsh. Nutrition was bad. People had very bad and little clothing. People started to get swellings on their hands and feet that winter. And for awhile people started to cut blankets to make pullovers and sweaters. They would hide them under their sheets and make gloves. The guards found out about that and there was a raid one day. Everyone who was caught having that sort of thing was taken to isolation cells where the conditions were even worse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These conditions, did they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These conditions, did they affect your health? Besides what you have already mentioned, that is, the loss of weight and the swollen ... Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the war started, I was a very healthy man, I had never been to see a doctor my whole life. But later, due to the fear and horrors that I experienced in that prison, and the conditions, I got very sick. I'm ill most of the time. I go to doctors and hospitals often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of illness did you get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got diabetes; inflammation of nerves in the leg and in my back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were in the KP Dom, was medical care available to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally. A doctor would come from the hospital. People would apply to the guards, but not everyone who applied could get to see the doctor. In the beginning a gynaecologist would come, Cedo Dragovic; and then after him a radiologist, Milovan Dobrilovic; then a general practitioner, Biljana Stankovic; then also Slobodanka Perovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone die due to the conditions in the KP Dom? Do you recall anybody? I mean the living conditions, not the other things.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, a group of people was brought in from Montenegro, from Herceg-Novi where they were captured. Those people had fled from military operations before the war, they had fled to Montenegro, and that's where they were captured and brought a busful of them to the prison. Among them was a young man. His name was Esad Hadzic, whose ulcer burst in his stomach. He had an ulcer perforation; he was in terrible pain when he died. Then I also know that Juso Dzamalija hanged himself in an isolation cell. Sefko Kubat died; Ibraham Sandal died. Omer Kunovac died; he was deaf and mute and they kept beating him. Although he couldn't speak, they wanted him to answer their questions, but he was deaf and mute. I know about that. An old woman died. She was isolated with two children and an elderly man in Room 11, when it had been emptied, and they found them somewhere, this old woman, two children, and a man, from somewhere in the village of Godjeno, and that's where this woman died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Esad Hadzic. When did he die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He died in June 1993 -- 1992, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he request medical help or did anyone request medical help for him when his ulcer burst?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. People from his room begged the guards to take him somewhere or to give him medicine, but nothing -- nothing ever came of that and he died in the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that woman. When did she die, and of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why she died, but she was a very old woman. And that first winter, 1992/1993, she was in that huge room without heating. We could see when food was brought to them in those small dishes. And one day she was just wrapped in a blanket, put on a freight vehicle and taken away somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Sefko Kubat, when did he die, and of what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a long time he suffered from a stomach ulcer. He was a thin man, but he worked the whole time, until he was in such pain that he couldn't work anymore. Then he was taken to a hospital for a surgery, and three or four days later he was brought back in the state in which he was, and he died there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the summer of 1994, around that time. I can't say exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Omer Kunovac. Of what did he die?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kunovac. From beatings. People that were in the room with him said that he died from the beatings, and he was completely deaf and mute.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did he die?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Ibrahim Sandal. When did he die, and why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was brought into the prison, he was unable to stand on his feet. He was black and blue and swollen all over his body. He would -- he never wished to talk about where he had been beaten and by whom. He was unable to go to the canteen, although the guards would force him, and he would go on all fours to the canteen; he had to. But he laid the whole time. And one morning they came to wake him up to go to breakfast but he was already dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. While detained in these two and a half years, were you always locked in the room or could you also go out for walks in the yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For ten months I couldn't get out of my room, they wouldn't let me. For a full ten months I was able to go only to the canteen and back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that only you, or was that the general conditions for all the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were taken out to work; some were in the labour platoon. But Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. most of us were not allowed out of the room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have family visits while you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two or three times my wife came. By mid-May, that is when visits were forbidden. In mid-May, all visits were forbidden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your wife visited you, did she need to have permission? And if so, where did she get it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she didn't need a permit. It depended on the guards, whether they would let her in and whether they would call me so we could see each other. Mostly they would come to the gate. They would ask, they would plead, they would ask whether they could see us. If someone would let them in, then we could see each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who made this decision? Was it just the guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. It could have been the guard; it could have been someone else. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get letters from your family in these two and a half years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a year and a half -- I mean during the first year and a half, I did not know at all where my wife and children were, where my mother was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What effect did that have on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for most of us, had it not been for the iron bars on the windows, half of us would have jumped out of the window. It killed us psychologically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you beaten at KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see other detainees being beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw that. I saw that. In the room, two or three times they would beat these detained persons, and in the rooms downstairs in particular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify. Do you mean in Room 15 itself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did this happen? Do you recall when you saw detainees being beaten in your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not any big beatings in the room. Usually they were taken to the administration, into the solitary confinement cells; that's where they did the big beatings. This was just beating in passing. If somebody asked a guard something, then he'd hit him twice or three times and then he'd go out and say, "No more talking."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)? Is my house still there?" And then he beat him up. Then Halim Corovic, an elderly man, was beaten, and then Ekrem Zekovic. That's what I saw in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness just mentioned the beating of Smajo Bacvic, and it's Schedule A-1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was beaten in your room? We're speaking now first about beatings in your room. Was there anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not in the room. Not in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness just said that there weren't any beatings but that these were just -- these were just people who were sort of hit in passing, and the Prosecutor keeps asking about beatings. And I think that the witness distinguished between this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The witness said there were not any big beatings in the room, and he also said that there were just beatings in passing. I don't see the problem of calling them beatings. We know what he means, and the description of them will probably bear out that limitation. But there's nothing wrong with the question. You proceed, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall any other particular incidents of beating of this -- let's call it lighter beating, in the room, in the prisoners' quarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this Halim Corovic. He was also beaten up there in the room. Then Ekrem Zekovic was beaten in the compound when we were going out for lunch. Predrag Stefanovic beat him in front of all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall Halim Corovic - that's the incident Schedule A, number 4 - do you recall who beat Halim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was a certain Muharem Cosovic in your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in number 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did anything happen to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out of the room and beaten twice while his little girl stayed with us in the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This is the incident, Schedule A, number 2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been the month of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that that did not only happen in your room but also in other rooms. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know because later people were mixed. I mean, they were being transferred from one room to another and everybody talked about what they had seen in their previous room, and the other people talked about what they had seen in their rooms previously, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned the big beatings, what you call the big beatings. Can you describe what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These guards, usually two of them or one of them would come into the room and then we would watch them. As they would come from the gate, when the metal gate would open, we would watch them, wondering what building they would go to, because we were in great fear. When he'd enter the building, he'd usually have a small list in his hands, and then we kept watching, and every room was in anticipation, wondering which building he is going to go into, which room. Let's say he first went into number 12 or number 14 or number 13, and then he went from one room to the another and called out persons' names. The main thing was that he'd have a list of these people whose names he'd call out. Then people would follow him. He'd lock up the room and then he'd take these people to the gate. We would watch them and we would see them standing in front of the gate. And then usually he would bring two or three into the administration building and the others would remain in front of the gate, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. waiting. Soon after that, it would get noisy in these rooms, in these visitation rooms. There weren't any glass panes on the windows. Whoever had the courage to listen could hear what was going on; however, most of us put pillows on our ears so we couldn't hear these cries and moans and screams. Few people were returned to rooms after these tortures; most were not returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "he," do you mean a particular guard who took the detainees out all the time, or is "he" just meant for many guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They worked in shifts. It depended on the day who was on which shift, and then that person would take people out. Whereas the others -- I mean, there were people there whom we noticed really took this out on people. They behaved as if they could hardly wait to take them out to be beaten. They would walk through the compound, you know, with their batons like this. They would whistle and they would take people away that way. They would carry these wooden legs of chairs, cables, all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can we have some description of what he was doing? It was very difficult to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The witness was moving his hand as if he had a baton in the hand and as if he --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said, you know a baton -- for example, when they would take a group out for this interrogation, then usually from the other building or from the factory or from the dining hall where they were, then these guards would probably -- most often withdraw and go towards the administration building. And then I would say that -- then as I said, for example, Milenko Burilo, who did horrible things there, he would usually carry a wooden leg of a chair, and there was a leather band on it and he would put it around his wrist, and then he would go to the administration building and then all hell would break loose in those premises where they took the people. There were some guards who really took it out on people, and we had the impression that they could hardly wait to beat someone and to beat someone up over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned already the guard Milenko Burilo. Can you tell us names of other guards who behaved in such a manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. As far as I could see, as far as we could see, Dragomir Obrenovic was among them, Vlatko Pljevaljcic, Vitomir Micevic, Jovo Savic, Predrag Stefanovic, Zoran Matovic, Radovan Vukovic, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what time of the day were detainees taken out in this manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually in the afternoon, and it would last until the evening, until 9.00 or 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it's difficult to remember after such a long time, but are you able to say at what hour in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. When we would hear a vehicle that had a characteristic sound, it was a smallish kombi van, when it would arrive in front of the administration building - and there was probably something wrong with the exhaust pipe and they did this on purpose, they did it on purpose - when we would hear this, then we would know that the beatings and the severe beatings would start. And they always threatened us with some kind of military police. If somebody would not admit something, confess something that they were charging him with, then they would threaten him with the military police, saying that if this person would not confess, they would call in the military police, and that it would not go well after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, but do you recall, was it in the early afternoon or late afternoon that this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Sometimes earlier; sometimes later. It wasn't specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned the list -- the guard had a list. Can you describe the list, what it was, what it looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was just a little piece of paper with people's names on it. We could not walk up to him to see what it said there. We saw that he had a piece of paper in his hands and that he was reading names from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you could hear these horrible noises from the visitors' rooms, which you have previously pointed out to us. Could you hear anything particular? So that you could, for instance, hear who was being beaten or who was beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not come to such conclusions who was doing the beating, who was beating these men. There was commotion, general commotion, and there were cries, there were screams. You could not recognise voices.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you hear anything that let you conclude who was being beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We only heard once when they took Zulfo Veiz out, who had been a policeman before the war in the city police, the town police, and we only heard them say to him, "Well, Veiz, tell us now how many Serbs had you beaten?" And we didn't understand anything after that. That's when they started beating him. We could not discern anything else, because several people were hitting him and the others. It wasn't that it was one man or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness is referring to Zulfo Veiz who is mentioned under C-29 [sic], Schedule C, and he's also mentioned in the count of the indictment -- in the incident, 5.27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Zulfo Veiz, was he taken out only once or several times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several times. He was taken to the administration building several times. And there was nothing noticeable on him, that he had been beaten, until the last time when he didn't return after that. The first few times he was taken out in the evening hours, in the afternoon hours. Allegedly he said that some of his colleagues, his former colleagues, Serbs, came to see him, and once he even mentioned some kind of exchange, that he would be exchanged for some policeman in Gorazde and that he did not want to accept that. Later they took him out, they started beating him, and he never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in Room 15, Zulfo Veiz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you could not see injuries on him when he returned these several times. Did he tell you that he was beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never said that. It would have been obvious on him. He said that they did not beat him then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this last time, do you recall when you saw him for the last time being led away and when you heard someone speaking to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. How could I not remember?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I mean when. Do you know when that was, that last time when he did not return?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was June 1992. I'm not that sure about the date. Perhaps I'll make a mistake, but I can't -- I mean, July or August, but it's July most probably. I can't be very accurate about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These big beatings, did they last -- how long did they last altogether? Over what period of time did they occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that lasted from May 1992 until October, these severe beatings and these exchanges of sorts. That is when most people were victims, in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any peak in this time period? Was there ever any particular time when this occurred the most? Do you recall anything? Maybe a month.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, this Vidovdan, on the 28th of June, that is when a large group was taken away. Then in September they were taken to pick plums allegedly. Then also this big exchange on the 30th of August, when they told us that there would be an exchange, when they separated people from the bus and half of them went missing. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let's first stick with the beatings, and we'll come to the exchanges later. You said Vidovdan, the 28th of June, that was a particular day. What did you see on this day? How many people were led away, and to which part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People's names were read out. They always brought some kind of lists from which they would read people's names and surnames. And then they would say to them, "Get your things ready, whatever you have, and get out of the room." For example, from Room 15, they would take out five people; from another room they would take ten people out. That's the way it was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear shots in relation to beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we heard them. When they took Zulfo Veiz and Kemal Dzelilovic, Fuad Mandzo, people like that. Some people even listened in the late evening hours, during the night, and they said that they heard bodies dropping into the river. However, most people hid away, trying not to hear this. We were never sure who would be next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I had asked you if you ever heard shots and you said yes to this question. Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you ever -- do you recall how often you heard shots in relation to beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't often that one would hear shots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have already mentioned -- on one occasion you mentioned Zulfo Veiz and Kemal Dzelilovic. That's the person on Schedule C, number 7. Do you recall who else was taken together with these two? Do you recall anybody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fuad Mandzo, the two Rikalo brothers, Mato Ivancic. I can't remember it all now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But does that relate to the shots you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard the shots when they took Munib Veiz out. Not Zulfo, Munib. Who else was there? At any rate, five or six men were taken out, they were beaten up, and later shots were heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Munib Veiz, that's C-28 and B-29; and Fuad Mandzo is C-16. After you heard the shots, do you recall anything else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is when some people heard these thumps against the water. It sounded as if they had been thrown from the bridge into the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall who else was taken out from your room in this manner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Room 15, that is the room from which the least number of people was taken out compared to other rooms. However, Krajcin was taken out. Before the war he was head of finance in the mine. Then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's C-14.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Murat Crneta was taken out; he was director of a factory. A boy from Gorazde was taken out, Said Kunduklija. A man from Srebrenica was taken out who was arrested in Montenegro; he was temporarily working in Montenegro. And there was this group of men from Srebrenica that was brought in, and from amongst them, one of them was assigned to Room 15. Things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Halim Konjo in your room, number 15?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not. He was in number 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also taken out. Allegedly he was killed immediately, on the spot, when he was being severely beaten. We heard his cries, and he never returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Halim Konjo, that is B-33 and C-13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Halim Konjo taken out only once and never returned, or did you see him --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, once. Once, once, I saw it once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Nurko Nisic in your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in number 12, in number 12, Room 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out several times and beaten, severely beaten. He could not even turn around at all. He and Mustafa Kuloglija, a teacher, they were beaten several times. Aziz Sahinovic as well. They never returned again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Nurko Nisic, that is the incident 5.27 and C-19.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Nurko Nisic return and did see what injuries he had, or did you only hear about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We saw him from the window when they were returning him. He was all swollen. He could hardly walk into the building from the gate. It was hard for him to move. He was all beaten up. Later on they took him out for this severe beating again and he was never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Sahinovic, did you see him --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's actually the incident 5.29, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him return, and did you see any injuries on him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He returned once and he was all beaten up then. And then he was taken out again, because before the war he worked in a bank called Privredna Banka. He was an official in charge of some kind of foreign exchange transactions. And he told us that they had accused him of having taken some foreign currency. He said to us that he could not take it because it was down there in the safes. And then the third time -- I mean, the second time they took him over there to the bank, to where he had worked before. Then the third time, in the evening, sometime in the evening, they took him, sometime after 10.00 they called out his name, and he never returned either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have found a mistake in the transcript, and I probably misspoke. It's on page 3425 of the LiveNote, and in relation to Munib Veiz, the incident in the Schedule is B-59 and not B-29. That was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have already mentioned Mr. Kuloglija. That's in Schedule C-15. What happened to Mr. Kuloglija? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him for many years before the war. He was a teacher in a primary school called Ivanko [phoen]. And he was said to have had a fight with a Serb in the tavern before the war and the story circulated in the town. He was then imprisoned in KP Dom, and he was taken out several times and beaten. He came, beaten up, back to the room twice, and the third time they took him away to another beating and he never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also mentioned Fuad Mandzo - that is number C-16 - what happened to Mr. Fuad Mandzo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Room 14. This is a young man who was allegedly captured in a village above the hospital. He was brought in, and I heard people say he was accused of being a member of the SDA party, the Democratic Action party, that he stood guard in the village of Donje Polje, where he lived; that he protected SDA leaders. He stood guard; he was their security, that is. They also beat him up and he never returned. They took him away once and he never returned after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if anything happened to another Mandzo in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Emir Mandzo, he was on the medical staff in the hospital. He was said to have been beaten up by mistake, they mistook him for another Mandzo. They also took out Salko Mandzo also by mistake. They told him it was a mistake, because the guard who came to pick him up, to call out Fuad Mandzo, he just said, "Mandzo," and took out Emir Mandzo. Salko Mandzo was also taken out by mistake, and only after that, the third time, they specified it was Fuad Mandzo and took out, indeed, Fuad Mandzo, who never returned after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Emir Mandzo you mentioned - that is actually B-36 and B-37 - was he in your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Emir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Emir, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in Room 16. After the beating they threw him outside to the asphalt. They couldn't -- he couldn't stand on his feet because they beat him on his soles as well. They just threw him out through the gates. He fell down on the asphalt, and then he was later picked up and taken to another building, to Room 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Salko Mandzo - that's actually the incident 5.28 of the indictment - was he in your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was in Room 12. And when he returned after that mistake, when he got beaten by mistake, we saw that he was bleeding below his eye. We looked from the window. There was blood trickling from below his eye. They told us that they had put a knife there, saying that they would gouge out his eye. And he was also beaten up by mistake; he was beaten instead of Fuad.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness now Schedule C, that is, Exhibit 55.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we have already discussed some of the people on this list. I would like now to talk about particular persons on the list. Do you know the person number 1, Alija Altoka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person number 3 -- we have already spoken about Bico Salem. The person number 3, Abdurahman Cankusic, do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him. He used to work in a company called Hidrogradnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him in KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did see him there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see him and when did you stop seeing him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him from the beginning until sometime in July or August. I'm not sure about the month, but it was one of those two months. And then he was taken away. And his brother Refik was taken away as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they taken for beatings? Was that such an incident when you heard beatings afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean for the two of them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of them were just taken away that day, beaten up, and they never returned to the compound. And their father was also imprisoned in Room 14 and listened all the time while they were being beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the person number 5, Enko Cedic, also referred to as Ekinda.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in Room 11, I think, or perhaps 13. He too was taken out repeatedly for beatings, and once they -- once they took him, never to take him back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have already mentioned Juso Dzamalija, and you said that he committed suicide. Can you tell us when this happened and what happened to him before he did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was shop assistant in a shop before the war, and his son, Ahmo, was deputy chief of police in Foca. And his son left Foca in those first days and the father was beaten because of the son, allegedly. And he was so badly beaten up, although I didn't see him myself, but I heard that he was so badly beaten up that during the night, that was in the beginning of May, I think, he hanged himself. And this nurse who was in my room, 18, I think it was at that time, this Gojko Jankovic, he told me in prison that he was summoned to take him -- to take him down in the isolation cell where he had hanged himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 8, Ramo Dzendusic, what can you tell us about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him personally because he worked in the National Defence Secretariat until he was retired. I don't know where he was captured. He was kept in Room 16. We saw him being taken out and we heard him being beaten, but he never returned. And there is no trace of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 9, Adil Granov.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was an electrical engineer, a youngish man, who was also taken away one day and never returned. I didn't hear him being beaten; we could not make that out. But the main thing is he never returned and there is no trace of him, no word of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 10, Nail Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a driver in the electrical company, an elderly man. But he was a member of the SDA, probably, and he was active during the establishment of the party. He too was taken out, and we heard him being beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the next person, Mate Ivancic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a Croat who was employed in the hospital as a medical technician. He was brought from his workplace in the hospital. They took him out. We didn't hear them beat him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 12, Esad Kiselica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a man who worked in the electrical company, an electrician, a sick man, youngish. He too was beaten and he never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now we can move on to number 17, Krunoslav Marinovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also a Croat from Foca who had a private television repair shop. He too was beaten. And during his arrest - I heard he was in Room 11 - I heard that before he was taken to prison, they broke his jaw so he couldn't go out to eat. And I didn't hear about any other beating. But in any case, he was taken away, never to return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 18, Omer Mujezinovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 20, Hamid Ramovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a farmer from Celebici whose brother was the first victim in Foca, a policeman, Abid Ramovic, who was killed on the 7th of April in Foca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Mr. Hamid Ramovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
