utterances.text: He too was repeatedly taken out, and we could hear him being beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he disappear as the others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the following three are all with the last name Rikalo. Can you tell us something about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know them personally. But they were in Room 11, and they were beaten on two occasions. After being taken out for the second time, they never returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All three of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. None of them returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 24, Seval Soro.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And 25, Kemal Tulek.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was a policeman in KP Dom. He was imprisoned and taken away, but I don't know about beatings. His brother, Ekrem, though, spent four or five months in an isolation cell and was transferred to Room 15, and even his next-door neighbours couldn't recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 26, Enes Uzunovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a fine young man, a medical technician, a youth activist before this, president of the youth association in Foca. They beat him several times. They kept him below the staircase in an isolation cell. He was isolated down there, below. They didn't keep him in rooms with other prisoners. And we heard him being badly beaten down there. We heard his cries. He was taken away later, I didn't see when, but he is missing. But he was beaten and abused several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he was kept in an isolation cell under the staircase. Where was he -- what isolation cell in which building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Building 1. Right after the entrance there is a staircase leading to the first floor. An isolation cell was built there with four cots. I peeped in once when there was no one around at a later stage. They kept him there for the whole time before they took him away. They kept him together with another man, Kemal Krkalic [phoen]. They kept them there for a long time before taking them away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, to clarify, when you say building 1, I rather would like to show you now the floor plan 6/2, to point out where this isolation cell was. First of all, was it on the ground floor or on a higher floor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground floor. Here you see the entrance to that building. This is the entry room, this is Room 12, then 11. Then the staircase leads to the first floor from here. Below the staircase, there is a landing here from which you go diagonally, and here on the ground was the isolation cell.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is pointing at a spot where the staircase is indicated on this sketch, between the Rooms 12 and 11.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here below the staircase.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the person number 27, Dzemal Vahida, if you look, please, again on the list. Can you tell us something about Dzemal Vahida?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dzemal Vahida, before the war, used to be a policeman in the town police. We saw him being brought to the gate, and while other people were being beaten, he stood at the gates waiting for his turn. And when he was brought inside, he never returned. I knew him as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, from all these people on Schedule C that you have mentioned and that you said they disappeared, did you ever hear anything about them or that their bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This -- you have mentioned at an earlier stage of your testimony that you heard these screams coming from the visitors' rooms in the administration building. Did you also hear such noises from other parts of the administration building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the new wing, the so-called new wing of the administration building, where, before the war, there used to be rehabilitation officers' rooms. They also beat and abused people there. Opposite Rooms 11 and 13, that's where these rooms are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This pattern of taking people out for beatings, how did this affect you and the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was insufferable to listen to. Only some people could stand to stay by the windows and listen, while most of us hid deeper inside the room, covered our ears with blankets. That was really insufferable. Few people could stand being by the window the whole time and listening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you fear to be taken as well for beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the whole time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you interrogated while in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at my own request. Because I had spent there ten days without being called to be questioned, and until I heard that those who did not make statements would not be allowed any visits, I kept quiet. But when I heard that, I started thinking and I realised I had been there for ten days without being called to give a statement. And once when I was standing there I heard -- I saw the warden come out into the compound. I stepped out and asked the warden why they had brought me in and were not calling me to be interrogated, and I heard that visits would not be allowed to such people, and he answered, "We'll see." After that we were taken back from the canteen to our rooms, and half an hour later, a guard came to pick me up and took me to the administration building to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the warden," who was the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Milorad Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did you know that at that time, when you approached him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew. Everybody said when we would address the guards on some issue, asking for some sort of assistance, of course we didn't dare address all of them, but there were among them people whom we did dare to approach and they would reply that they couldn't decide without the warden. It was known that he was the warden. Everybody knew that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you approached him and talked to him, did you address him as Mr. Warden or did you address him with his name; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I stepped out of the line, I approached him, and I told him, "Mico, what's this all about? Why is nobody calling me?" I addressed him by his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why you were in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without giving any names now, were you the only person who approached Mr. Krnojelac on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion I was the only one who approached him. I don't know about people from other rooms. But on that occasion I stepped out of the line and approached him, because he wasn't very far away from us, perhaps 4 or 5 metres. He was passing by. In fact, he was standing there by a tree within the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he alone on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was his son there as well and a guard. I don't remember which guard. But his son was there. And I approached him on another occasion, because my mother and brother lived in Donje Polje and I lived in the centre of town, and before, while I was at home, my telephone was disconnected and I didn't know what was happening with my mother. She's completely unable to move and almost blind. So on that occasion when I saw the warden standing there, I approached him and I asked him to allow me to go out and see if my mother was still alive, because I didn't know what was happening in Donje Polje. All the houses were burning or burnt down. I didn't know whether my mother's house was still standing. And he told me to go to lunch and he would see, that's what he said. And later Slavko Koroman came to my room, Room 15, and asked me out. So I went out and his -- that is, Milorad's son was in the car, in a camouflage uniform, while Koroman was in civilian clothes. The two of them drove me to my house where my mother and brother were; however, I didn't find my mother there because she had been taken to hospital. I found my brother at the neighbour's; he didn't dare stay in the house alone. He told me that nobody came for him, that my mother had been taken to the hospital. And both times I had asked to visit my home he made it possible for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This time when you approached him to get information about your mother, when was that? Was it after your first approach to Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when, when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this happened in May, in early May, because I was taken away on the 23rd of April. We still had visits at that time, so it was the first half of May, because on the 15th of May, they banned all visits.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said -- how often altogether did you approach Mr. Krnojelac, two times or three times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only those two times. And later when I was transferred to work in the furniture factory, he would come with some delegations who toured this factory and we would just say hello when he passed by. No more than that. You couldn't call that a meeting. I just saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that his son was with him. Which son? The son Bozidar that you have already mentioned, or another one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Bozidar. I really don't know their names, but I think that was the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of a function did he have in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the guards said he was his personal security, but I don't know about that. In any case, he was wearing a camouflage uniform and carrying an automatic rifle. He was very strongly built. I don't know his real name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said, "He was his personal security." Whose personal security?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the warden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interrogated, where did that take place, and who questioned you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I addressed the warden of the prison, a guard came and called my name out, as well as the names of two other persons from the room next door. So it was three of us who were brought to the gate. We entered the administrative building, and that is where these inspectors were, these inspectors who were in charge of these interrogations: That was Zoran Vladicic, Vojislav Starovic, Miodrag Koprivica, and Petko Gasevic. They interrogated all these men who had been in prison. When the three of us were brought into this administration building, Zoran Vladicic, a former investigator in the criminal police in SUP before the war, he said to me at the door, "Where is your Boro Kujundzic?" I was friends with this chief of police before; we visited each other at home even. And I said, "How should I know?" and he said, "You'll know. You'll know." And he cursed my mother, this Zoran Vladicic did. However, Miodrag Koprivica said to me, "You come with me," and he took me through the hall of this administration building to a door. There was a door where it said "Accounting." He took me in this room. Since I knew him personally, I asked him, "What's this all about, Miso?" and he said, "See what's happened?" I sat there. He ordered me a cup of coffee and he let me light up a cigarette, and he asked me sort of where I was those days until I was brought in, from when the attack on Foca started until I was brought to prison, so that I would tell him where I was during those days. I told him about this a bit, and he typed this out on a typewriter. It was half a page or a page. He let me read this text and I signed it in four copies. I read it; I signed it. It was nothing terrible. I mean, he wrote it the way I said it, where I was during those days. I signed it. He didn't give me a single copy. They didn't give copies to anyone; they left all of them there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you accused of anything particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that there was a report against me, and I said, "What kind of report?" and he said that it said that I was shooting from the court building. Since the building was near my building, I mean this court was, it was as if I was shooting from there, and Zulfer Pjano, the public prosecutor from that building - Zulfer Pjano was the name of this public prosecutor - that he and I were shooting from the court building at other buildings. And that public prosecutor had escaped to Gorazde even before that. Throughout the war he was in Gorazde; he was not there at all. And I said, "Miso, how could I shoot? How could I be in the court building?" and he said, "Zufer and you." Zufer I knew was in Gorazde. (redacted). I know that he escaped with his wife and his child to Gorazde. And he said, "Well, all right. Of course, I doubt that you did it too," and that was not even recorded in this statement of mine. I signed this statement in four copies, and he kept all four copies and sent me back to the room, Room 15, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were interrogated, were other detainees interrogated in adjacent rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, these two who were brought with me. One was interrogated by Vladicic, I guess, and the other one, by Starovic. The one who was interrogated by Vladicic was the Halim Corovic I mentioned, this elderly man. I heard him moaning that Vladicic had beaten him. I heard these moans and cries from the next-door office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the third man? Was he mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the third one. I don't know who the third one was. I don't know. He was brought from another room. Out of this fear, I couldn't ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear anything in relation to this third person? What happened to him? Was he mistreated, or didn't you hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These policemen who interrogated you and the other two, were they -- how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian clothes. They wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that Ekrem Zekovic was beaten in the yard on one occasion. Did you ever see anyone else being beaten in the yard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see detainees being beaten on the way or in -- on the way to the canteen or in the canteen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that, that they were beaten. But from Room 15, we could not see, because a group barged in. And another room was out for lunch, and then as they were coming back from lunch, this group barged in and then they started beating them as they were passing by them. But I didn't see this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the group that barged in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that detainees were exchanged. Were these detainees seen afterwards again or are they missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most people who were taken for these so-called exchanges went Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. missing. I know that because they did not reappear in the compound, and until the present day, there's been no trace of them. I also see in the papers that their families are still looking for them, until the present day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your brother with you in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Two of them, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they together with you in your rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your brothers? Are they still with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was exchanged together with me two and a half years later. He was brought in to prison from hospital, from where he had worked, in his white uniform. Seven doctors and seven medical workers were detained; there were 14 members of the medical profession in the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). We were told that this group was being taken away for a real exchange, and I was happy that at least he was taken away to be exchanged. And it turned out that he's the one who never reappeared again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How big was the group of people that were taken for exchange on the 30th of August? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fifty people were put on this bus. After I got out of this prison, I found out that this group had been stopped somewhere near Niksic and then they were returned to the KP Dom again. They spent the night there and that is where they singled out a group of some 20 younger men. They were taken away and there's been no trace of them since. This other group of some 30 men was exchanged somewhere in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you try to locate your brother? Did you search for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After getting out of this prison, I tried all around, through different people, in Serbia, even in Pozarevac. A friend of mine looked in that prison there, but there's been no trace whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the brother you are talking about, is that the person who is on the list in front of you, on Exhibit P401? Is that the brother you are talking about who is missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that medical staff was also detained in the KP Dom. Do you know a Dr. Aziz Torlak, and can you tell us what became of him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aziz Torlak, I knew him personally. He was taken away sometime in 1993 for some kind of an exchange, and he never returned again, nor does his family know anything of him. I don't know what happened to him. Everybody assumes that he's been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that a detainee once escaped from the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the way it was: It was in the first half of 1993. I don't know the month now but it was in the first half. This one group of men, craftsmen, metalworkers, they were taken to this so-called metal plant that was outside the confines of the prison. That's where they worked. The rest were returned to the compound, and he escaped. This went on for about three days, but then they caught him and brought him back. They caught him somewhere on the road leading to Montenegro. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this escape have any consequences on the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it did. When they caught him and brought him back to prison again, we were forbidden to work. Nobody could get out of the room. There was torture those days until we were -- until he was caught. They halved these small meals we were getting; they took away our medicines, whatever we had. They hardly had anything to take away from us. They forbade us to get out of our rooms. There were no medical examinations. They carried out this raid, as they called it. When they brought this Zekovic, they took us out of the room and they lined us all up on the grounds. They brought him in front of this line, and Savo Todovic talked to us there before the warden. He said that no one should dare escape, that not even a bird was able to fly across; that he was caught, he was not beaten, that's what he told us; and indeed we did not see any traces of violence on his face, because he was not far away from the line, 2 or 3 metres away from us. The warden was there, Krnojelac, in front of us, in front of this line-up, that is. There was Miro Prodanovic, commander of the guards, this guard service, and Savo Todovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Mr. Krnojelac do? Was he just standing there or was he also addressing you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was just standing there. He was just standing there. He didn't say anything. Only Savo Todovic spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were forbidden to work when this happened. So at that time you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, most people worked. Some worked on the prison farm. There were farms for chickens, cattle, cows; it was an agricultural farm, what do you call it. Others worked in a mine; yet others worked in the furniture factory; others worked on cutting wood; others were gathering hay; others were repairing Krnojelac's house, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to know what you worked. What were your assignments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having spent ten months in the room, I could not take it anymore psychologically. I asked a guard how I could get in touch with the warden. He said to me, "Write a request. Write that you want to have an interview with the warden," and that's the only thing I wrote: "I wish to have an interview with the warden." And the guard took it, and two or three days later a guard called me out of my room and he took me to this small room at the entrance of building 2. Right by the entrance there's this small room where a guard sat, during the night as well, and that's where I found Savo Todovic. The warden did not want to see me. This Savo received me. When I got out, skinny as I was, I could hardly stand on my feet, and he said, "What do you want?" "I want to go out and work." I pleaded with him, even in that condition, just so that I could go and work. I couldn't take it, being locked up in a room anymore. And he said, "What are you going to do when you can't?" and I said, "Anything. Just let me go out into the compound so that I get a bit of air. I'll go crazy," I said. And he said to me, "Well, we'll see," and he returned me to the room. After that there was lots of snow. Lots of snow had fallen. A guard called me and informed me that I was assigned to work on piling Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. firewood within the compound and carrying it to the canteen, to near the kitchen. I carried it for days and days, this frozen firewood, and I was very lightly dressed. It was so hard for me to do it, I could hardly do it, but it was only important for me not to be in the room. And this went on until spring, until we ran out of wood. Some people were cutting this firewood, and I was piling it there. And then I was assigned to the furniture factory. In the meantime, I was taken from time to time to the farm to work on the cornfields, and also to gather hay for the cattle. But for the most part I spent my time at the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever donate blood while in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, once. Once. This was at the beginning, when this prison medical official was going round the rooms, saying that blood should be donated, that there wasn't enough blood at the hospital. There were wounded persons there; there were Muslims, Serbs, children; there were quite a few wounded. And over 40 of us signed up then. A team came from the hospital, from this transfusion department, and we donated blood and we were given a pack of cigarettes each, a pack of fruit juice, and a sandwich, respectively, and then we were returned to our rooms. The other time he asked no one signed up. People were so exhausted that nobody dared do such a thing anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now move to the command structure in the KP Dom. You have already mentioned that Mr. Krnojelac was the warden. Why was -- do you know why the former warden was replaced by Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why the previous warden was replaced. This is a man I knew well. He probably thought that it was not the right place for him. I think that's what he did. He was a smart man. Hardly anyone would accept something like that, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This former warden, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radojica Tesovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he remain on the prison staff? Did he do something else instead of being --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of the farm. He was outside the compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do we know what his ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I didn't hear you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do we know what his ethnicity was?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radojica, what ethnicity? He was a Serb. A Serb from Celebici, from Zavajt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who appointed Mr. Krnojelac in his position as a warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who appointed him. I assume it was the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you approached him twice in the prison. Did you see him more often in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, when he would come in. During the day we worked in the factory. Perhaps he came in several times but I would only see him when he came to the factory, to tour the factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing when you saw him in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore a military uniform, an officer's uniform of the former Yugoslav army, that reserve officers had; without insignia, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, you have already described that his son was with him. Who else was with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean then, when I addressed him? Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In general. When you saw him or when you approached him, who was with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, when I approached him, his son was there and some of the guards. I can't remember who. But as he was coming to the factory to tour it, only the guards were there. His son was not there; his son did not come in. There were other soldiers with him, some other soldiers -- some other guards who were on duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said he toured the factory, what do you mean by this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would come with men unknown to me, probably buyers of this furniture. I don't know who it was. But at any rate, they passed through the factory; they looked at this furniture that we were making. We would just say hello in passing and he would pass with them. He would not stop to talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you approached him twice. Do you know of any other detainee who had conversations with him, with Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long was Mr. Krnojelac the warden?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until 19 -- until the half -- until mid-1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who replaced him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was replaced by Zoran Sekulovic from Godjen -- the village of Slatine, who was before the war employed in the Oslobodenje, a newspaper company in Sarajevo, in the marketing department, I guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the conditions in the KP Dom change after the replacement of Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The abuse stopped and the attitude of the guards improved. They were not so rigid as before. They gave us more bread, which is the most important thing. And we did feel a change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put to you at that point something that the accused says about his position. He said that the KP Dom, during the war, had two separate sections, a military part and a civil part. The Muslim detainees were in the military part and the normal convicts were in the civil part, and he was only responsible for this civil part. Can you comment on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is nonsense; that is not true. There was no military part there whatsoever. All the people there were civilians. There was only one man, and I mentioned him before, who had been captured on his position and he was exchanged later with us. There was no other part. All of it was civilian. So that is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I don't know whether you're going to follow it up, but he in that answer was dealing with the people who were being detained there. I thought you had asked him about the people who were running the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So I think you should follow that up.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. I intended to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, it's not -- Mr. Krnojelac does not argue that you were prisoners of war or involved in any military actions. He only says the prison, as such, was actually two different compounds, a military prison and a civil prison, and he was only dealing with the civil prison, that is, with the normal convicts and not with the Muslims. The question is: Was there such a division into a military part and a civilian part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the military, only Serb soldiers were locked up; in building 2 they were kept. And there was no one from the Muslim army, no military Muslims. And those people were kept there because they were rowdy or drunken after being out all night. Those Serbs were kept down there because they refused to go back to their positions. But he was warden for the entire complex. Everybody knows that and everybody will confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that you ask him directly: Were there any military people who were running any part of the prison? That's what we really have to know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the Presiding Judge. Was any part of the prison, whatever part, run by the military and not by the civilian staff and Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know that, whether there was any military administration over this prison, because from my position I was unable to find out; nor have I ever seen any military officer enter the compound, ever. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have described to us Mr. Savo Todovic. What was his function?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he was the so-called officer for employment of former inmates, and later, at the time we're talking about during the war, while we were there - I don't know what his position was called - but he decided who would go to the mines to dig, who would go to other types of work. Nobody could decide that without him; no guard dared to do anything without his approval.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he wearing when you saw him in the prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he wore a military uniform; sometimes civilian clothes. It depends. But he often wore some kind of military fur coat, and that's the nickname he got, Bunda, which means fur coat. And when people saw him, they knew there was going to be trouble; everybody was afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he wear a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He often carried a pistol. You could see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he beat detainees or abuse them otherwise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he beat them. When Zekovic tried to escape, he interrogated the people who had worked with Zekovic in this metal workshop, and he beat most of them, as if they had known that he was going to try to escape and as if he had planned the escape. That's what he tried to insinuate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the guards, that's what he was called, was Mitar Rasevic, and he held that position even before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he treat the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, he didn't do any bad things then. He often entered rooms, advised us not to try to do anything stupid. But I never saw him beat anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk with him personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Mitar? I did once, when a neighbour of mine, a woman, brought me a shirt, some underwear, from my apartment. That's when I spent some time with him, when he invited me to collect this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him whether he knew how long this madness was going to last, and he told me to keep quiet, to act normally, not to try anything. He told me, "Nobody will hit you." That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk with him about the bad living conditions in the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were detained until October 1994. How many detainees were exchanged together with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty-eight. There were 68 of us in that last group from the KP Dom. And from Rudo, from Batkovici, there were people as well from those places. It was a large exchange on that day. We were the last to get out of the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you meet your wife and your family again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A month after the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did she leave Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She left in August, I think, August 1992. She was given an exit permit from Dragan Gagovic allowing her to leave Foca together with the children. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the exit permit which has the identification number in the trial binders of 127 and 127A. I would like to show him the B/C/S version. You can have this one. Please do not put it on the ELMO because the names are on there. THE USHER: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you look at this permit from the 27th of June, 1992, is that the name of your wife and your children on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to enter this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Those documents will be Exhibit P127 and P127A; they will both be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall that you gave a statement to the investigators' office on one occasion and that you, on this occasion, handed over a list with the names of the prison staff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you made this list, did you make it from your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, based on my memory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this list you gave the name of -- the names of about 12 guards Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you mentioned that they stood out in brutality; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you repeat for the Court the names of these particular brutal guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Maybe not all of them but I'll try. Milenko Burilo, Dragomir Obrenovic, Vlatko Pljevaljcic, Vitomir Micevic, Predrag Stefanovic, Jovo Savic, Radovan Vukovic, Milovan Vukovic, Zoran Matovic - him especially, and Burilo as well, and so on. I can't remember any more at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have described to us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you have described to us how you suffered while you were there and that you also have some permanent results -- permanent physical damage. Do you still suffer psychologically?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Often in the night I wake up screaming and I'm soaking wet. It's very difficult for me to shake off this state. I tremble frightfully. It's horrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are all the questions that the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination, Mr. Vasic? Perhaps I should remind both you and the witness, when you're both speaking in the same language, you do tend to get ahead of the translators, so pause at the end of the question before the answer commences, and pause at the end of the answer before the next question commences.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Vasic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to introduce myself to the witness. I'm Miroslav Vasic, one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Krnojelac. Since you started your testimony on the 9th of November this year, when you took the solemn declaration, and today is the 23rd of November, can you please tell me where you spent this time between these two sessions of the court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this period, did you talk to anyone about the subject of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first part of your testimony you mentioned that, together with the accused, you were a member of the Territorial Defence. You also said that he had a higher rank than you did. My question is: In the army establishment, were you superior to Milorad Krnojelac in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The commander of the staff was his superior. (redacted) (redacted). And he was a commander of a very large unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your place there, your position in the institution where you said you worked, are you aware that in 1994 [as interpreted] there was a reorganisation in the unit which was, until then, commanded by Milorad Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went to drills after that and he continued for another two years in that position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that he was replaced on that position by Mr. Radovic, who became commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radovic? No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you perhaps remember that you were at a drill in 1992 [as interpreted] together with the accused on the stretch from Zavajt to Godjen Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who was the commander of that drill, his full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the drill?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the drill was the then colonel from the district headquarters in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, please do wait. You're well and truly ahead of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what was the ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the colonel?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, do you know where Milorad Krnojelac's house was at the beginning of the armed conflict, in which area of Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. In Donje Polje, above the carpentry shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that his house was burnt down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear that some other Serbian houses burnt down in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, just to get the picture clearer, you asked -- or at least you are recorded as having asked about this colonel who was a Muslim taking over in 1994. Did you mean 1984? Was it before or after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1984, yes, certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked about the drill in 1982, who commanded that drill, and who took over command of the detachment in 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, but I don't see the transcript from where I'm standing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's gone, and I don't have a laptop in this courtroom, but it definitely said 1994, which seemed curious at the time. You may or may not have said it; it may have been a misinterpretation or a mistyping. But I thought I should get it cleared up. You are talking about before the war, and that's all we need to know at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was your house burned down during the military operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's still standing. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Donje Polje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to answer this? Well, in any case, you can see the entrance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just a moment. There is a problem with the question of identification. If you'd like, we can go into a closed session to get the detail if you really need it. We've been redacting most of the references to where he lives. But there have been references to him being able to see the fish restaurant, and I understand that. If you want to go into some detail, I think we should close the court for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I would kindly ask that this be done, because this is important. It refers to the statement of this witness. The position of his apartment is relevant; it's important for us to know where it is and what can be seen from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, we'll go into closed session. It will take just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, we're in public session now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the question of the Prosecutor, you said you gave a statement to the investigator of the Prosecutor's Office.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really understand. Did I what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When asked by the Prosecutor, you said you gave a written statement to the investigators of the Prosecutor's Office; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you read that statement and sign it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With that statement given to the investigator of the Prosecutor's Office, did you also provide your manuscripts related to some staff of the KP Dom and a list of persons employed in the KP Dom from 1992 to 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I gave that only in order to clarify certain things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In those manuscripts you gave then, did you write about a person by the name of Savo Todovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll now read out to you what you wrote, and you will tell me whether you have, indeed, written this and signed this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is page 13 of your attachment. I will read slowly because I think the interpreters don't have this text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Should the witness have a copy of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The interpreters have this document and they can read from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I should think so, yes. But that should not be an invitation for him to speed up, though, please. Could somebody take it across to the witness? Thanks. You are showing him page 13, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On this page, I will start with the part following the basic personal information about Savo Todovic: "In the words of his associates, some of whom were inmates in the camp, he stood out even then in maltreating former inmates. On the part of the command of the Serbian army, he was appointed the man in charge of Muslim detainees, which he constantly proved by his actions. He enjoyed this role, and every time he appeared in the compound, that was fatal for the majority of prisoners. He ordered people to be beaten, maltreated, and killed, and he frequently participated in this himself. "He also distributed prisoners to work in various places such as the mine, the felling of trees, work in the factory or on the farm, hay-cutting, clearing up the rubble, et cetera. He often participated personally in the search of rooms and put people in solitary cells for minor infractions. Without his approval, nobody could be released. He frightened prisoners out of their wits." Did you write this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it is time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you stated that when you came to the KP Dom, when you were brought into custody there, that the guards were the former guards of the KP Dom. Do you remember having said to the investigator of the Prosecutor's Office that when you came to the KP Dom, that there were some paramilitary forces there that came out of that region, out of Foca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. But there were some people. There were even some former prisoners, Serbs. There were a few of them, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Today you stated that some of the soldiers -- some of the inmates made underwear out of blankets, made underwear. Was that possible if everybody just had one blanket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was more than one blanket until they searched the rooms. When they realised that people were cutting up these blankets -- I don't know how they found out, but when they searched the premises, they took everything away from everyone and left every person with just one blanket apiece.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when this was, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the winter of 1992/1993, when we did not have any fire, when we did not have any heating at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your stay at the KP Dom, did you get an infusion from the doctor who was there also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not from the doctor. When I lost consciousness three times, then Gojko Jokanovic brought me an infusion in the evening, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dr. Amir Berberkic, our doctor who was detained in our room, put the drip on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me who Gojko Jankovic was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he worked at the KP Dom as an x-ray specialist, and he retired in that position. But while we were there, he was the man in charge of the clinic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us in which room Kemal Dzelilovic was, as well as Fuad Mandzo, Zulfo Veiz, Munib Veiz?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Kemal Dzelilovic was in Room 12; Fuad Mandzo, number 14; Munib Veiz, in number 11; Zulfo Veiz, in number 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- I mean, you said that they were taken out. When did this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first months of our stay in prison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they taken out together when they never returned or individually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken out individually. They were not taken out all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the time when each and every one of them was taken out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date right now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they taken out on the same day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zulfo Veiz and Munib Veiz, I think there were two or three days in between.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Halim Konjo, whom you also mentioned today here, when was he taken out and where was he taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken to the administration building, and rumour had it that he had been killed, that he had succumbed to the beatings. From Room 12, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the administration building," is that the visitation area that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the rest, the other prisoners? Were they taken to the administration building, to that area for visits?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean for giving statements?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I mean the beatings that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean to Munib Veiz --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the names. They went very fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did you get that message, Mr. Vasic, from the interpreters? They said that you are speaking the names far too quickly and they cannot really keep up with you. So if you could repeat the name, or at least pause after each one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If counsel could just pause after the witness' answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I did not get this message, but I shall bear this in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was Kemal Dzelilovic, Fuad Mandzo, Zulfo Veiz, Munib Veiz, Salko Mandzo; were they taken to these same premises for beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you stated for Salko Mandzo that he was taken out of Room 12.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell the investigators of the OTP that he was taken out of your room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I did not. I don't think I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are saying that he was taken out of Room 12.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, out of Room 12.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you talked about an exchange that took place when one group of prisoners was taken to Montenegro and returned. Do you recall having said to the investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor that this group was separated in Niksic; that in Niksic the younger prisoners were separated from the others, including your brother, and that they were taken away from somewhere and that they are registered as missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have said so. Possibly I did, because I did not know the truth. Only later, when I met some people from that group, they told me how it all went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall now go back to the documents that you handed over to the investigator of the OTP, that are handwritten by you, that is, document 7, the list of Serb employees in KP Dom Foca.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Item number 1, you wrote -- actually, item 1 says: "Krnojelac, Milorad - warden of the prison."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milutin Tijanic, deputy.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milan Vojevic, deputy. Very briefly. I heard that he left very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Todovic Savo, officer in charge of work distribution, commander appointed him to be in charge of camp inmates."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what he told us when Ekrem Zekovic escaped, that he was appointed by the military commander -- oh, what's this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Both of you, would you please wait until the translators have had a catch up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that the court reporters cannot keep up with the speed of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall put my question again - thank you, Your Honour - so that it would be in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point 4: "Savo Todovic, officer in charge of work distribution. The Serbian commander appointed him to be in charge of camp inmates."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you are reading, you do speed up quite naturally. It's something which everybody does without realising it until it's pointed out to you. So when you are reading something from there, remember to keep your speed down. Then please, sir, will you wait until -- if you can hear the translation going in the background there, wait until you hear it stop before you answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This same person said to us, when Enes Zekovic had escaped -- no, Ekrem Zekovic. When we were lined up there, he said that the Serbian army put him in charge, that he was to be in charge of the detained Muslims and that he could kill all of us because he has 400 bullets for his automatic rifle, and that he alone could kill all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Item 5, it says: "Radojica Tesovic, director of the Drina production unit."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, from which date or from which time was Radojica Tesovic director of this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know. That I don't know. He was at the farm but I didn't know. I didn't go up there then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you said that you saw Milorad Krnojelac going towards the fish restaurant. Why did you not mention this fact in the statements that you gave to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor and the other statements that you gave to the Security Centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these same statements, why did you not say that you thought that Milorad Krnojelac was a member of the SDS, but you did say that here before the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember why I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, Defence counsel read to you what you have written in your summary about Savo Todovic, and also in your list, that he was in charge of the camp inmates. What did you mean by him being in charge of the camp inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS FWS-66 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that he's the one who said who would work where, which room people would be transferred to, because guards brought lists in and said that that is what he had ordered.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please say something else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, if you wish. If you want to sit down so it can be heard properly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. But, really, I did not come here to bring charges against Todovic or even -- or Tesovic or even Krnojelac. But after everything we've been through, I would kindly ask this Court to find out where all these missing people are. There are so many children who are orphans nowadays. There are hundreds of them. Even until the present day, they've not found out where these people's bones are. Can we at least bury their bones? The families don't know until the present day. They hope that some of them might appear some day, but I realise that all of them have been killed. But let's be told once and for all where they were killed. Let this be investigated. It is sad when I and the other people watch on TV Bosnia-Herzegovina the warden of the KP Dom stating that he does not feel guilty about any one of these counts. Let him say where all these people are. He was the warden there; he should know where they were taken and where they were all killed. That is what I wish to say. I really do apologise to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, sir, I can tell you you are not the first person who has expressed very similar sentiments to the Tribunal. We, of course, are restricted to the issues which arise in this case. But what you have said has been noted. We thank you very much for having expressed your views, but we have to leave it there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, is yours the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. The next witness is Mr. Jussi Kemppainen. He is an investigator at the Tribunal. Briefly, the evidence that he will be giving is evidence as to the inquiries made as to the disappearance of individuals named in Schedule C of the indictment, and also in relation to the interview of the accused. He will be referring to a large amount of documentary material which perhaps doesn't need to be referred to at length. But before he comes in, if I can just identify the material that he will be using in his testimony so that no confusion arises. In relation to the inquiries as to the whereabouts of the detainees at KP Dom, that material is contained in binder 3 of the potential Prosecution exhibits. And that material, I would ask that that be identified as Prosecution identification number 55/1. Originally the binder was given the number of 55, but that Schedule in front of the binder that relates to the indictment was given that exhibit number, P55, just the Schedule. So if the binder could be referred to as 55/1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The whereabouts or the inquiries as to the whereabouts of all of these people, that's a matter that was raised during the Pre-Trial Conference. As I understand it, the Prosecution is not being put to formal proof, so that could just be tendered, could it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that's what I -- that's, in fact, what I would like to do rather than go through this file one by one and take an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There are just a couple of documents within that that need a small amount of clarification, a couple of typographical errors. So that should take a brief amount of time. Similarly, with the interview, there's the videotapes, the transcripts, and a couple of documents that were referred to in the interview. That material is contained in binder 2 of the Prosecution potential exhibits, obviously apart from the videotapes. But just briefly, in relation to the material of 55/1, there's a couple of extra investigator's notes that are provided to the Defence today, and we've provided to the Court. The first investigator's note relates to Salem Bico, which is number 2 on the Schedule, and that simply is a replacement of the same investigator's note that appears in binder 55/1 except it's been redacted. The details of the person that gave the information, the phone number, et cetera, has been taken off. So it's just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But that has been given to the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That has been given to the accused this morning. This is just three extra --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you said "some material has been redacted," is there an unredacted copy for the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it's been redacted for the purpose of taking away the details of the phone numbers, of the current whereabouts of that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then that's a replacement. And then there's two additional investigator's notes that should be placed in binder 55/1 and that is in relation to Krunoslav Marinovic; he is number 18 on the Schedule. Also an investigator's note in relation to Munib Veiz, and he is number 28 on the Schedule. These two investigator's notes are the only two notes that won't be reflected in the index at the front of this binder, 55/1. Also, this investigator has some materials which were provided to the Defence and to the Court with an index attached to it, and they relate to results of inquiries of the whereabouts of detainees that were not -- are not in Schedule C, not those 29, but six extra people that were in the KP Dom, and those -- that information arose out of the particular inquiries for these 29 individuals. And that packet of information, it's about 20 pages or so, it has an index in the front of it, and that is entitled, that index: "Inquiries as to the disappearance of other KP Dom detainees not listed in Schedule C of the indictment," and I would ask that that be marked 55/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you propose to amend the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we're not -- I think in the indictment we've taken the position that we would prove the killings of the 29 in the Schedule, but in the general wording of the indictment, I think we also -- we also state that in addition to the 29 individuals named, other individuals are also murdered at the KP Dom, or the KP Dom was a significant contributor to the death of these individuals, and I think we've kept it broad in that regard. We have specifically put ourselves to 29, but there is, I think, wording in there that allows for these other individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Marinovic, by the way, is number 17, not number 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bakrac, first of all, there's a replacement for Salem Bico, and then there are the two additional matters. Have you any problems in relation to those, the notes, the investigator's notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And then there's the folder with the six additional people in Schedule C -- I'm sorry, people not in Schedule C. Have you any problem with that material?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, since the Prosecutor said that they are going to keep 29 persons, that they are not going to amend the indictment accordingly. So we do not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I don't want there to be any misunderstanding about that. What they're saying is that there's a general allegation in the indictment which says the 29 people in Schedule C and some others they have been unable to name. Well, now they are able to name some additional ones. They are still relying upon the general allegation in the indictment. So have you any problem in relation to this material which is marked or identified at this moment 55/2?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in that respect, we would have to check this material out. We would have to check the statements or allegations made. We would like to see whether this document could be admitted into evidence as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. Will you be able to have those investigations completed by the time we resume at the beginning of next year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so, Your Honour. We have enough time to try to investigate this. I cannot exactly envisage this, but I should think that December should be sufficient for establishing all of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you really take no issue, as I understand it, with their death, you only take issue with the means or the manner of their death, it should not be too hard for you to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I would like to add something to what you've said. You said "manner of their death," but also place of their death, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I accept that. Well, Mr. Smith, we might leave that one marked for identification at this stage, but bearing in mind the way in which the others have been dealt with, it's unlikely there will be any problem about it. I think the Defence should be given the opportunity of making some investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They may find somebody alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right, then. Well, then, the material which is presently in the folder will be Exhibit P55/1, and the other material will be marked for identification 55/2, at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you want to tender the transcripts and videos?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this might be a quicker way of going about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I would ask that the transcripts numbered 43, 46, 48, and 50 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Wait a minute. 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: 46, 48, and 50, which reflect the four days of interview with the accused, that they be tendered. Copies have been provided to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, They're in the binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right, yes. And the videos -- the corresponding videos, 44, 45, 47, 49, and 51, that they be tendered. Videotape 44 and 45 relate to the first day of interview; that's transcript 43.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bakrac, the investigator is going to be here for you to ask any questions of, but do you have any objection to the tendering of that material?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. The objective of our -- of this interview has been to make it helpful, and there is no reason for us to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you've certainly managed to get in everything that you've wanted, I think, having read most of it. Well, those transcripts will be Exhibits P43, P46, P48, and P50, and the videotapes will be Exhibits P44, P45, P47, P49, and P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And there was five documents that were referred to during the interview: a map, which was marked by the accused, which is a redacted map -- the map that, in fact, was marked was not redacted of the Witness 12 who made the three-dimensional drawing of the KP Dom, but we have a redacted version of that map with the marking that the accused placed on it, and I would like that that be tendered as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Has it got a number now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It has no number now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection to that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P402.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then the list of the guards was referred to, but that's in as evidence already as P3.
